newsitem.title: USA: Dole to meet Israeli leader Netanyahu Wednesday.
newsitem.headline: Dole to meet Israeli leader Netanyahu Wednesday.

text.p: A delicate Middle East summit became enmeshed in the U.S. presidential election campaign on Tuesday when Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Republican candidate Bob Dole scheduled a meeting.
The meeting, originally set for Tuesday, was postponed until Wednesday evening at Netanyahu's request, said Dole spokesman Nelson Warfield.
Dole, trailing President Clinton with only five weeks until Election Day on Nov 5, issued an unusually critical statement of Clinton's foreign policy a day before the summit.

Clinton called the summit with Netanyahu, Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat and Jordan's King Hussein to rescue the Middle East peace process, after an explosion of violence in Jerusalem, the West Bank and the Gaza Strip last week that took the lives of 57 Palestinians and 15 Israelis.
Finding himself thrust into the background yet again as Clinton took centre stage, Dole blasted the administration for conducting "photo-op foreign policy."
He also warned Clinton not to put pressure on Netanyahu, saying: "Our friend Israel must not be asked to make concessions as a means of restoring order (in the Middle East)."
For Netanyahu, the meeting with Dole might also be seen as a form of political payback, after Clinton openly backed his Labour Party rival Shimon Peres in last May's Israeli election.
The right-wing Netanyahu has close ties to leading U.S. Republicans, including vice presidential nominee Jack Kemp.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry, in the middle of a lengthy briefing on the summit Tuesday afternoon, said "It's not worth taking time" to respond to Dole's criticisms.
"The president was doing very, very hard work today. I think Senator Dole in his heart of hearts knows that," McCurry told reporters.
"I can understand his frustation and wanting to try to make some news today, but I'll leave aside his comments and try to stay focused on the work the president's doing," McCurry said.
McCurry said, however, that it was "very appropriate" for Netanyahu to meet with the Republican party nominee.

Earlier, McCurry said Dole should examine Clinton's record before making assessments, saying Clinton had been able to provide leadership in the Middle East peace process "precisely because we have fulfilled our commitment to our longtime ally Israel."
Dole spokesman Warfield took a swipe at Clinton's support for Peres during the Israel election campaign, while defending Dole's words.
"His comments have been entirely appropriate, rather unlike President Clinton's remarks about the recent Israeli elections," Warfield said.
Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle said Dole was coming dangerously close to interfering with Clinton's conduct of the nation's foreign policy and should back off.

"I think Bob Dole is getting closer and closer to the edge and perhaps close to crossing the line in a very, very sensitive area of international involvement for the country today," he told reporters.
"Pronouncements and charges of siding with one or the other this close to a negotiation has the potential of doing damage to these negotiations in a very serious way," he said.
Richard Haass, a Middle East adviser to former President George Bush, said Dole should have also offered to meet with Arafat and Hussein as well as Netanyahu.
He said there was little danger Clinton would put heavy pressure on Netanyahu this close to the election.
"Five weeks before an American election is not the time to twist Israel's arm," he said.
Polls show Clinton leading Dole overwhelmingly among U.S. Jews. Dole has tried to narrow that gap by closely allying himself to Israeli conservatives.
